claims.claim: Historical thinking is the practice of reasoning about the past like a historian — asking questions and constructing evidence-based interpretations — rather than memorizing names and dates.
The Stanford History Education Group's 'Reading Like a Historian' framework centers on four historical-reading skills: sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, and close reading.

Sourcing asks who created a source, when, and why, and evaluates its trustworthiness; contextualization situates a source in its own time and place; corroboration compares a source against others to establish what is probable and to notice where accounts diverge; close reading analyzes the author's claims, evidence, and language.

Sam Wineburg founded the Stanford History Education Group in 2002 and argued that historians critically analyze documents and authors' motives while American students of history are too often relegated to 'searching for facts,' identifying sourcing, contextualization, and corroboration as key heuristics.
Wineburg's book 'Historical Thinking and Other Unnatural Acts: Charting the Future of Teaching the Past' was published by Temple University Press in 2001 (ISBN 9781566398565).

The Library of Congress teaches primary-source analysis through an Observe / Reflect / Question routine: observers collect what they notice, reflect by connecting observations to prior knowledge, and question to plan further investigation.

The National Archives teaches a repeatable document-analysis progression — meet the document, observe its parts, try to make sense of it, and use it as historical evidence — that stays the same across every type of source.

History is interpretive: historians distinguish established facts from interpretations, and disciplined accounts of the same event can differ because they are arguments built from and accountable to evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many core 'historical reading' skills are named
positions: SHEG's Historical Thinking Chart lists four skills: sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, and close reading
Wineburg's foundational research most often names three heuristics: sourcing, contextualization, and corroboration
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are correct and complementary. Close reading is the fourth reading skill added on the classroom chart; the three-heuristic version is Wineburg's original cognitive framing. The lesson presents all four and notes close reading underlies the other three.

sourceRecords.title: Historical Thinking Chart (Reading Like a Historian)
sourceRecords.provider: Stanford History Education Group / Digital Inquiry Group
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. The chart (originally SHEG, now hosted by the Digital Inquiry Group) defines the four historical-reading skills used in the lesson: SOURCING (identify author's purpose/position and evaluate trustworthiness), CONTEXTUALIZATION (understand how the historical period shapes a document), CORROBORATION (compare documents to establish what is probable and notice disparities), and CLOSE READING (identify claims and evaluate evidence and reasoning). Marked © Digital Inquiry Group; materials gated behind login. Reference-only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Historical Thinking and Other Unnatural Acts: Charting the Future of Teaching the Past
sourceRecords.notes: Publisher page and ERIC record ED457103 confirm: Sam Wineburg, Temple University Press, 2001, ISBN 9781566398565, part of the 'Critical Perspectives on the Past' series; won the 2002 Frederic W. Ness Award. Wineburg founded the Stanford History Education Group in 2002. Used for his framing that historians analyze documents and authors' motives while students are relegated to 'searching for facts,' and for the sourcing/contextualization/corroboration heuristics and the fact/interpretation distinction. Book text not fetched; bibliographic facts and framing corroborated via the Temple UP page, ERIC, and Wikipedia. Reference-only.

sourceRecords.title: Historical Thinking Skills Guide
sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Open educational resource describing historical-thinking skills including sourcing, contextualization, comparison, causation, continuity-and-change, and claim testing, and framing history as making and testing evidence-based claims rather than memorizing facts. Page footer shows a copyright notice without an explicit CC license, so treated REFERENCE_ONLY; facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Document Analysis Worksheets
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-19. U.S. government teaching resource (public domain). Teaches a repeatable four-step document-analysis progression — meet the document, observe its parts, try to make sense of it, use it as historical evidence — that stays the same for every type of primary source, plus an 'Understanding Perspective in Primary Sources' worksheet on how backgrounds and beliefs shape point of view. Used for the structured-analysis-routine content.
